entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Pearl of Great Price is a foundational text within the canon of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS), first published in 1851 in the United States. This work is significant as it serves as a theological and scriptural touchstone for millions of adherents globally, encapsulating essential doctrines, revelations, and a history that the church considers integral to its faith. Key figures associated with its production include Joseph Smith, the founder of the LDS Church, and various early church leaders who contributed to its compilation and interpretation.

The text itself consists of several distinct sections, including the Book of Moses, the Book of Abraham, and the Articles of Faith, which together provide insights into creation, the nature of God, and the purpose of life as understood by Latter-day Saints. First published in Nauvoo, Illinois, the Pearl of Great Price has undergone various editions and revisions, with its current form being standardized in 1981. The text is not only a source of spiritual guidance but also a reflection of the socio-political context of 19th-century America, where religious movements were emerging and competing for influence.

The legacy of the Pearl of Great Price extends beyond its religious context, as it has influenced discussions on American religious pluralism and the nature of scripture. The text has played a significant role in shaping the identity of the LDS Church and has helped to establish a distinctive narrative that separates Latter-day Saints from other Christian denominations. Its teachings continue to resonate, fostering a unique cultural and spiritual heritage within the church that persists into the modern digital age.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Pearl of Great Price has shaped the religious landscape for millions, influencing the identity and practices of the Latter-day Saints, a movement that now spans the globe with over 16 million members. Its theological assertions continue to provoke scholarly discussion and community reflection on faith and doctrine.
